To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the colon has a low capacity to oxidize acetaldehyde compared with other tissues of alimentary tract, and the capacity of colonic ALDHs to oxidize acetylaldehyde is low compared with hepatic ALDHs.
rat colonic mucosal cytosol, mitochondria, and microsomes contain low amounts of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrog enase activities.
rat colonic mucosal cytosolic aldehyde dehydrogease (ALDH), with a low affinity for the substrate, is able to remove acetaldehyde produced in the colon by bacteria.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the metabolism of alcohol by the human gastrointestinal tract.
the study of the role of the colonic microflora in the development of colonic diseases.
the study of the role of alcohol dehydrogenase in the metabolism of ethanol and acetaldehyde.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ALDH activity of rat colonic epithelial cells is sufficient for the removal (detoxification) of acetaldehyde generated by colonic epithelial ADH during ethanol metabolism.
colonic mucosa possesses sufficient ALDH activities to remove the acetaldehyde formed by colonic ADH during ethanol metabolism.
colonic mucosal ALDH activity may be sufficient for the detoxification of the acetaldeyde produced by the colonic mucosal ethanol metabolism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ALDH activity of colonic mucosal cells is not enough to remove the amount of acetaldehyde that is produced by intracolonically residing bacteria during the oxidation of ethanol.
the colonic mucosal ALDH activities are sufficient for the removal the acetaldehyde formed by colonic mucosa ADH during ethanol metabolism.

the colonic mucosal capacity to remove acetaldehyde produced from ethanol by colonic bacteria is low, and this could lead to accumulation of acetaldehydes and contribute to the development alcohol-related colonic damage and cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
colonic mucosa has the ability to oxidize the acetaldehyde that is produced in the colon by intracolomic bacteria during ethanol oxidation.
ALDH2 and ALDH3 are the two most abundant isoenzymes in rat colon.
the colon is not a major site of acetaldehyde formation from ethanol.
